title: Cuthbert and the Dewdrop Diamond
markdown:
Cuthbert was a rabbit of precision. Other rabbits were content to nibble clover and twitch their ears at the breeze. They found a juicy dandelion and called it a perfect day. Cuthbert brushed his whiskers until they stood like silver wires, kept his paws spotless despite the soil, and treated his greenhouse as a kingdom that must not wrinkle. All season he had nursed his prize tomato plant. He had named it Crimson Majesty, as if a grand title could keep fruit perfectly round. He had spent a week fretting over a single speck of dust on a single leaf.

Each dawn he performed the same small ceremony. He aligned the watering can with the path's third brick. He counted leaves. He spoke, very quietly, to Crimson Majesty about weather and patience, as if the plant kept minutes. One dewy morning he opened the door. Warm air came out to meet him, sweet with ripening tomatoes and damp earth, a perfume that made his chest lift like a souffle that had decided to behave. Condensation jewelled the glass. A robin tried the roof and thought better of it. He approached the finest fruit, the one destined for the Village Fair's Blue Ribbon, and his nose, which he trusted more than weather, gave a nervous flutter.

On the tomato sat a dimple. Tiny. Almost invisible. To Cuthbert, it was an insult to geometry.

He puffed his chest at a cucumber that had never once offered an opinion. "An anomaly," he told it, theatrical as a pigeon in a gust. "It requires immediate personal attention. No one else would grasp the nuances."

Dignity, in Cuthbert's private dictionary, meant solving problems without admitting he did not know how to mend a mysterious dent. He printed a card in his finest nibbled lettering:

DO NOT TOUCH. PRIZE TOMATO UNDERGOING CRITICAL REPAIR BY HEAD GARDENER. ASSISTANCE NOT REQUIRED.

He propped it beside the fruit, aligned to the nearest paving brick, and nodded. Respectable problem-solving. He even stepped back to check the alignment from a second angle, because one angle was never enough.

Bram the cat padded in, tail hooked into a question mark. He loved Cuthbert even when the fussiness made no feline sense. He read the sign, with its shouting importance. He looked at the tomato, which appeared to be minding its own business. He looked at Cuthbert pacing, ears dipped a fraction, a rabbit trying to look taller than his worry.

"Hello, Cuthbert," Bram said, a rumble like far-off summer thunder. "What's all this about critical repair? Did the tomato have a little ouchie?"

Cuthbert cleared his throat. "A minor structural anomaly. Specialised skill. Mine, naturally." He gestured at the sign with a paw that wanted to look casual and failed.

Bram squinted, emerald eyes mild. "So you don't want me to smooth it with my paw? When my fur gets ruffled, a gentle lick helps. Very soothing."

"Absolutely not." Cuthbert's whiskers vibrated. "Your assistance would be counterproductive." He rather liked the word. It sounded like a tool you could hang on a hook.

"Counterproductive," Bram repeated, tasting it. "Worse?"

"Precisely."

Cuthbert took the soft-bristled brush he used on delicate leaves and prodded the dimple, expecting it to pop back into polite roundness. It did not budge. Not a millimetre. It felt smooth, strangely cool, and caught the morning as if it had been waiting for someone patient. He leaned until his whiskers brushed a neighbouring leaf and the greenhouse smelled suddenly of wet glass.

It was not a dimple. It was a miniature globe of dew, frozen by the unusual chill of the morning and clinging like a jewel that had chosen this tomato on purpose.

Cuthbert, still loyal to his own idea of perfection, treated the jewel as a new problem to be banished. He produced a pocket rule from behind a seed packet and measured the fruit twice, hoping the dimple would confess to being a trick of the light. It did not. He flicked it with the brush, then with a fallen petal from a nearby bloom. Nothing. The dewdrop clung, as if it belonged. He even tried a puff of breath, warm and careful, the sort he used on fogged spectacles. The globe only shone harder. In his fluster he jostled the branch. Crimson Majesty's prize fruit wobbled, teetered, and leaned toward the hard floor with the slow drama of a disaster that had found its appointment.

Bram's tail twitched. He leapt to the bench, a ginger blur, tail out as a counterweight. The tomato steadied. Then a paw, precise as a librarian's finger, brushed the frozen dew—not to banish it, but to polish it. The little jewel brightened until even the cucumber seemed, for a moment, interested.

Cuthbert's paws hung in the air. He had braced for a crash, for ruin, for a year of explanations. The tomato was safe. Beside the stem sat the dewdrop, serene, catching the window like a miniature diamond that had decided to stay.

Bram sat and groomed a paw, as if rescue were an ordinary Tuesday and Tuesdays were not to be discussed.

"You didn't remove it," Cuthbert whispered.

"Why would I? It looks rather lovely. Like the tomato is wearing a tiny sparkly crown."

Cuthbert looked properly this time. A little crown. He had been so busy defending roundness that he had missed the morning's gift. Bram, who asked about ouchies and believed in licks, had seen it first.

They stayed a while in the hush that follows a near-miss. Water ticked in the can. A bee bumped the glass and went away, unoffended. Light moved across the brick path in a slow gold bar. The air smelled of wet soil and sweetness. Cuthbert did not make a speech. He watched the dewdrop hold the window, and the sign that forbade help looked suddenly like a joke he had told only to himself.

The Village Fair arrived on a crisp autumn day, pies steaming, villagers bustling, marrows lined up like sleepy boats, judges stern behind magnifying glasses. Cuthbert carried Crimson Majesty as if it might bruise from a glance. For one foolish second he nearly wiped the dewdrop away with his cuff, returning the fruit to the roundness he had worshipped all summer. Bram looked at him. Cuthbert lowered the cuff. He presented the tomato with a heart that felt surprisingly unbuttoned. They praised size and colour. Then their eyes found the dewdrop, still there, a misplaced star on crimson skin.

"Remarkable," said the head judge, adjusting his spectacles. "A most unusual and captivating feature. One of a kind."

Bram pretended to nap in a sun patch near the table, which fooled nobody who had seen him leap. Crimson Majesty did not win the Blue Ribbon. It won a special commendation for Unconventional Beauty, written in ink that caught the light almost as well as dew. Cuthbert stood beside his friend and felt a warmth that had nothing to do with glass and soil. In his pocket the old card still forbade assistance. He did not post it on any bench. He only brushed a whisker straight, then left it slightly crooked, and went to find the pies before they vanished into more organised mouths.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
